paras: The police shooting of Chris Brooks took place in Wilmington, Delaware, in August 1890, when Officer Sherer used his revolver while arresting Brooks, a Black man charged with stealing chickens, and wounded him in the leg. The shooting became known when the city solicitor mentioned it at Brooks's hearing in the Municipal Court on August 18, and the case was postponed for a week so that the wound could be treated.

Brooks, described as "colored," was arrested on a charge of stealing chickens; the date and place of the arrest are not given. According to City Solicitor Lynam, Officer Sherer "was obliged to use his revolver" in making the arrest, "inflicting a wound on the prisoner's leg." The solicitor did not say what Brooks had done to make the shot necessary, and no account from Brooks or any witness appears.

When Brooks came before the Municipal Court on the morning of August 18, Lynam asked for a one-week postponement and for Brooks to be moved to the almshouse so that the wound, which he called "a slight one," could be treated. The court granted the postponement. No report of the later hearing or of the outcome of the chicken-theft charge was found. No report of any inquiry into the shooting appears in the coverage.

The shooting is known from one paragraph in the Wilmington Evening Journal's "Municipal Court" column, whose headline listed a drugged girl, "A Friendly Quarrel" and "Several Drunks" but not Brooks. The paper placed the item among routine cases of drunkenness and petty theft and repeated, without comment, the solicitor's statement that the officer had been obliged to fire. No other white paper and no Black paper was found to have reported the shooting.
